brief: Nvidia's board reversed itself and returned Jensen Huang as CEO, leaning on government assurances while the investigations into him and the company's chip sales are still open.
The chip-smuggling thread runs through the day: the Megaspeed listing, the criminal probe behind it, and Huang's return all concern the same supply chain.
Anthropic is pushing autonomy deeper into the coding loop, with Claude Ship approving routine pull requests and Code Mode letting Claude Code script its own tool calls.
AI products are getting a harder security test: states sue over Grok's image output, researchers chain flaws in Meta's Muse, and OpenAI and Cisco ship a runtime to shield unpatched Linux systems.
Open models keep trying new architectures, from Z.ai's looped transformer to NVIDIA's diffusion language model and Tencent's million-token Hy4.

stories.headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO eleven days after he resigned
body: Nvidia's board voted to bring Huang back as chief executive and chairman, reversing its refusal to take him back that it had announced only days earlier. The company said the move took effect immediately and rested partly on input from senior United States officials, who told the board his return posed no national security risk.

That assurance sits awkwardly beside the record the board was weighing. Huang has admitted an affair with a woman that US intelligence sources believe was working for China, and Nvidia faces allegations that it helped chips reach China in defiance of export controls. Several federal departments have open inquiries into those matters, along with accounting and governance questions, and none of them has been closed.

Huang began pressing for his return almost as soon as he stepped down, and President Trump publicly backed him, calling the reinstatement the correct decision and saying Huang did nothing wrong. Trump also argued that losing leadership of that calibre would be a bigger threat than anything tied to the China allegations. The board has tied its reversal to comfort from government, not to any finding that clears Huang, so the investigations now carry more weight than the reinstatement itself.
takeaways: Watch the Commerce Department's Megaspeed action, since it targets the supply chain at the centre of the chip allegations.
Track whether the open federal inquiries into Nvidia are formally closed or quietly dropped; a closed case would settle the board's reasoning, and an open one would not.
stories.source_title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
stories.author: Kyle Orland
stories.dek: The board cited government assurances of no national security risk, even though investigations into Huang and Nvidia's chip sales remain open.

stories.headline: Anthropic's Claude Ship lets AI agents approve routine pull requests on their own
body: Anthropic has launched Claude Ship, a set of agents aimed at the bottleneck that appears once AI writes much of the code: review and approval. Code Review is now generally available, while two new agents, PR Steward and Claude Approvals, are in beta. The package is rolling out to Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub.

PR Steward handles the chores around a pull request: failing CI checks, merge conflicts and feedback from Code Review. After every push it posts what it changed and how to roll that back. Claude Approvals is the part that can actually sign off. A team writes its approval policy as a file in the repository, in natural language, and the agent can weigh Code Review findings or Anthropic's own classifiers before it approves.

Anthropic's own guidance is to run approvals in observe-only mode first, start with a single repository, and set monthly spending limits. Teams keep control of where the agents run, which review depth they use, and which changes get escalated to a person. The open question is whether a written policy can separate the risky change from the routine one reliably enough to remove a human from the loop, and the beta is where that gets tested.
takeaways: Before turning on Claude Approvals, write the policy file and compare the agent's decisions in observe-only mode against what your reviewers actually did for several weeks.
Start with one low-risk repository and set a monthly spending cap before expanding it.
stories.source_title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes
stories.author: Sarah Perez
stories.dek: Approval policies live in a repository file, and teams can run the agent in observe-only mode before letting it merge anything.

stories.headline: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal
body: CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire the network security company Zscaler in a deal valued at $43.9 billion, paid entirely in stock. Coverage describes it as CrowdStrike's biggest acquisition yet and one of the largest in the sector, and it places the deal within a wider consolidation of security vendors as businesses try to keep up with AI-powered attacks. This story was written from the headline and the opening of the report, because the full article was not retrievable, so the figures are as reported rather than checked against filings.

CrowdStrike's chief executive, George Kurtz, pitched the merged company as one place to roll out AI, to supervise it, and to let autonomous software operate without putting networks at risk. Closing is pencilled in for late in CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028, which leaves a long regulatory and integration runway. Because the consideration is stock, Zscaler shareholders will be exposed to CrowdStrike's share price between now and closing.
takeaways: If your organisation buys from both vendors, ask each for a roadmap covering overlapping products and renewal terms before the deal closes.
stories.source_title: CrowdStrike to Buy Zscaler In $44 Billion Deal
stories.author: BeauHD
stories.dek: The deal would be CrowdStrike's largest acquisition to date and is framed as a response to AI-driven attacks.

stories.headline: Z.ai's GLM-5.4 reuses its layers in loops, and its weights are not open yet
body: Z.ai has released GLM-5.4, the first flagship from the company to reuse a block of layers in a loop. Each forward pass pushes the same shared-weight layers through several times, and the company argues that this makes the network effectively deeper while its size stays fixed. The same idea appeared days earlier in Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini, which runs its middle layers three times per token.

Simon Willison, who tested the model, reports that the weights are not public and that GLM-5.4 could not be reached through the standard API at launch. He got access by subscribing to Z.ai's coding plan, which shares an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with the regular API. He built a small plugin to use it and noted that an existing plugin would cover the model once it was updated. In his informal test, asking for SVG drawings of a pelican, the newer GLM generations looked much more like output from OpenAI or Anthropic models than the earlier GLM versions did.

The claim that matters is whether looping the layers buys real capability for less compute than a larger conventional model, and nothing published so far lets outside researchers check it. Without open weights there is no independent measurement of latency or serving cost for a looped architecture, so the comparisons the company makes against larger models stay on trust until someone can run the model at scale.
takeaways: If you want to try GLM-5.4, go through the coding plan endpoint, since the standard API did not support it at launch.
Watch for the open-weights release; it is the only way to measure the real serving cost of a looped architecture.
stories.source_title: GLM-5.4: Toward generalized coding with our first loop transformer
stories.author: Simon Willison
stories.dek: The new flagship is Z.ai's first attempt at looping a block of layers, and early access runs through a coding subscription rather than the standard API.

stories.headline: Virginia and Oregon sue SpaceX over Grok's sexualized images of real people
body: Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, which bought xAI earlier this year, over Grok's image generation. The complaints allege that Grok keeps producing non-consensual intimate images and child sexual abuse material from real photos, mostly of women and children, well after the problem surfaced. The company is now dealing with the fallout from the rollout of Grok's "spicy mode," a feature that generated large volumes of harmful imagery soon after launch.

The states say the safeguards were initially so weak that Grok sometimes produced nude images without being asked. The companies eventually apologized and said new safeguards and policies had been added, but the attorneys general argue those statements were misleading. They also say the team responsible for red-teaming Grok was cut to two or three people, and that the company could have tested outputs thoroughly before launching the feature.

The complaints stress that the harm lasts. Once an image is shared it is hard to remove, and victims may suffer anxiety, depression and reputational damage. Because Grok is integrated into X, the states argue that minors as young as 13 may have seen the content, potentially re-traumatizing victims of abuse. The case targets what the model itself generated rather than what users posted, which makes it a test of how much responsibility a company bears for its own AI output.
takeaways: If you ship image generation, test your safeguards against the same failures alleged here: unprompted nudity and sexualized edits of real photos.
Watch whether the attorneys general seek injunctions, which would force changes to the feature itself rather than only settle damages.
stories.source_title: States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn
stories.author: Ashley Belanger
stories.dek: The states allege that the company's public safety fixes were misleading and that Grok still produces child sexual abuse material.

stories.headline: Claude Code gets experimental Code Mode, where the model writes JavaScript to drive its tools
body: Anthropic has added an experimental Code Mode to Claude Code. Rather than issuing tools one by one and digesting every output, the model writes a small JavaScript program that batches, filters and sequences its calls to Bash, Read and Edit, handing back only what it needs. The mode ships disabled. Users have to run a recent Claude Code build and set an environment variable to turn it on, and Anthropic says the design may be reworked or pulled in any update.

The permission model is the detail to read first. Deny and ask rules and hooks still apply to every call a script makes. The difference is in auto mode, where a classifier vets the script as a single unit before it executes and cannot see anything the script works out along the way. Hooks now have to inspect every segment of a compound command, since a push can arrive chained behind a directory change. A project's own config file cannot turn the mode on, so opening a cloned repo cannot silently enable it, and an admin can switch it off centrally.

Support is narrow: interactive terminal sessions of the native build, not print mode, the Agent SDK, the VS Code panel, the desktop app, Bedrock, gateways or zero-data-retention organizations. Anthropic has published no token or latency figures. One outside comparison across eight interactive runs found identical results each time, with context 20 to 25 percent smaller and 37 percent fewer tokens on a larger task. It was not faster, and it cost more on a tiny task.
takeaways: Before enabling it on a shared machine, check your hook rules against chained commands, since they are the part most likely to be silently bypassed.
Measure on your own work: the one comparison showed savings on large jobs and extra cost on small ones.
stories.source_title: Claude Code Adds Experimental Code Mode to Orchestrate Tool Calls with JavaScript
stories.author: Daniel Dominguez
stories.dek: One script can batch and filter Bash, Read and Edit calls, and one independent test found smaller context and lower cost on large tasks, but no speedup.

stories.headline: Amazon pays $7.5 billion for Decart's optimization stack and team
body: Amazon has agreed to acquire a large part of Decart, the Israeli startup known for real-time interactive world models and AI video generation. Bloomberg reports the price at $7.5 billion. Amazon will take over the technology behind Decart's optimization software, along with its founding team and its AI researchers and engineers.

The asset that matters most is the Decart Optimization Stack, software that helps AI models run efficiently across Nvidia, Amazon and Google hardware. Amazon's framing is that cost is the main lever: more efficient compute means better training, faster inference and lower prices for customers.

The timing is the point. Amazon has used its Trainium chips mainly in its own data centers and is preparing to sell them to outside customers as an alternative to Nvidia. Software that makes workloads run well on Trainium without heavy rework is what would make that pitch credible. Decart and Amazon had not responded to requests for comment when the report was published, so the terms beyond the reported price remain unconfirmed.
stories.source_title: Amazon snaps up Decart’s AI optimization tech for $7.5B as it prepares to sell Trainium chips
stories.author: Rebecca Bellan
stories.dek: The deal brings in Decart's software for running models efficiently on Nvidia, Amazon and Google chips, along with its research team.

stories.headline: Anthropic lets enterprise customers keep Mythos and Fable prompts on their own servers
body: Anthropic is rolling out an early version of a system called Enterprise Frontier Safeguards to business customers, changing how it handles prompts and responses from its Mythos and Fable models. Customers still have to retain that data for 30 days, but they can now store it on their own servers rather than on Anthropic's.

The policy had been a sore point. When Anthropic launched version 5 of those models, it said it would keep prompts and responses for 30 days to catch misuse. Enterprise customers pushed back, and the pressure grew once OpenAI announced zero data retention for its own service. Anthropic had earlier signaled it would not enforce the same rule for its latest Opus model, and it later said it was building a system that would combine zero-retention privacy with stronger misuse detection.

Under the arrangement, Anthropic says it checks for signs of cyberattacks about every 15 minutes. If the automated systems flag a problem, the customer is notified, and Anthropic receives an alert too, but the company says it cannot access the underlying data. That is a narrower promise than true zero retention, and it depends on detection methods the company has not described in detail.
takeaways: If you use Mythos or Fable under an enterprise contract, ask whether the agreement covers customer-hosted retention and what storage the 30-day window requires.
stories.event: anthropic data retention enterprise frontier safeguards
stories.source_title: Anthropic softens its data retention policy for Mythos and Fable model use
stories.author: Igor Bonifacic
stories.dek: The 30-day retention requirement stays, but the data can now sit on customer servers under a system called Enterprise Frontier Safeguards.

stories.headline: Meta's Muse assistant could be hijacked from one malicious webpage, researchers show
body: Researchers at NebuSec found a chain of flaws in Meta's Muse, a cloud-hosted personal assistant that acts on users' accounts and services, and showed that a single crafted webpage could start it. The attack could expose conversation history, stored memories and credentials on the machine running the assistant. Meta fixed the reported issues before the research was published, and there is no evidence the flaws were exploited in the wild.

Each user's Muse runs in its own virtual machine, with a credential system meant to keep authentication details away from the agent and a monitor called Sentinel that watches outgoing traffic. The chain got the assistant to export the malicious page as a document, using the Chromium browser it relies on for that, which gave code execution inside its runtime. The attackers then used a known weakness in how Sentinel handles outgoing requests to send conversation history and memories to an external server.

The same route let an attacker rewrite what Muse had stored, including conversation history, which means the assistant could be made to hold false beliefs about its user. The lesson for agent builders is that each control can look sound on its own while a document renderer offers a way around both the sandbox and the egress monitor.
takeaways: If you connect agents to personal accounts, treat document rendering as an untrusted code path and check whether it can reach stored credentials.
Test whether any process inside your agent's sandbox can bypass your outbound-traffic monitor.
stories.source_title: Meta Muse can be hacked to access user private chats using just a single malicious web page
stories.author: Sead Fadilpašić
stories.dek: The chain exposed private chats, stored memories and cloud credentials, and Meta says it has patched the issues the researchers reported.

stories.headline: Ladybird ships its first alpha, a browser on its own engine for macOS and Linux
body: The Ladybird project has released its first alpha, a browser whose engine was built from the ground up rather than forked from another codebase. It is available for macOS and Linux. The browser around the engine is deliberately modest, and the team warns that some websites won't work and the app will sometimes crash, with a built-in way to report broken sites.

The change that matters most to developers is the rolling release channel. Automatic updates will ship regularly, so testers no longer have to build from source to follow progress. Ladybird also supports WebDriver for automated testing and the Firefox DevTools protocol, which means web developers can check their sites against a new, independent engine.

The team makes no security promises yet. It says every new browser gets hacked and asks researchers to report how they break in. Whether the project can attract enough web developers to find compatibility gaps quickly will decide how fast the engine matures, and that matters more than any single benchmark.
takeaways: Test your own site in the alpha and file what breaks; it is the fastest way to see where a non-Chromium engine fails on real pages.
Don't use the alpha for sensitive browsing until the team starts making security claims.
stories.author: Andreas Kling
stories.dek: The alpha will crash and break some sites, and the team is inviting security researchers to try to break it.

stories.headline: Megaspeed, tied to the Nvidia chip scandal, is headed for a US Entity List blacklist
body: Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud and AI infrastructure company, is expected to be added to the Commerce Department's Entity List, according to Semafor. Once listed, US companies would need a special federal license before doing business with it or selling it products. The reported aim is to cut off its access to US-made semiconductors.

Megaspeed was led for more than two years by Alice Huang, the woman at the centre of the alleged espionage affair involving Jensen Huang. During that period it was one of Nvidia's largest chip customers. Commerce recently opened a criminal investigation into the company, and authorities in the US and Singapore are both examining whether it evaded export restrictions to ship Nvidia chips to China. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing.

The listing lands on the same day Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO, which makes it an early test of whether Washington's comfort with Nvidia's leadership extends to the company's supply chain. Commerce had not commented when the report was published, so the listing itself is not yet official.
takeaways: If you buy from or sell to Megaspeed, or to companies that depend on it, check the Entity List before the next shipment.
stories.source_title: Megaspeed, the company at the center of the Jensen Huang scandal, appears headed for a US blacklist
stories.author: Lucas Ropek
stories.dek: US companies would need a federal license to do business with Megaspeed, and a criminal probe into chip smuggling is also under way.

stories.headline: Claude Fable 5.2 cost about three times Opus 5.5 in a bug-fixing test with similar results
body: VentureBeat ran both models through 15 bug-fix tasks. Fable 5.2 passed 10 at a total cost of about $89, and Opus 5.5 passed 9 at about $29. The outlet says a one-task gap is too small to separate the two, so the practical finding is the price difference. No model, at any price, passed the hardest task. This story was written from the headline and standfirst only, because the full article was not retrievable, so the figures are the outlet's and unverified here.

The pattern suggests that spending on the top tier buys little extra on routine bug fixes, though a sample of 15 tasks is thin evidence for any tier decision. The fact that both models failed the hardest task also means that neither one is a substitute for a human on the difficult cases.
takeaways: Before picking a model tier for coding agents, run your own bug set on both and compare cost per passed task, not just pass rate.
stories.source_title: Claude Fable 5.2 cost three times as much as Opus 5.5 for nearly the same results in a VentureBeat bug-fixing test
stories.dek: In a VentureBeat pilot, the top model passed 10 of 15 fixes for about $89, against 9 of 15 for about $29 from Opus 5.5.

stories.headline: DeepMind's agent teams cut quantum algorithm costs, with every result proved in Lean
body: Google DeepMind used teams of its Gemini 4 agents to improve well-known quantum algorithms, producing circuits that need fewer resources. The circuits target simulations relevant to fusion energy, chemistry and drug design. Because today's quantum hardware is too small to test these circuits directly, the team proved each result correct using Lean, a formal theorem prover, and is releasing the Lean library, problem specifications and verified solutions on GitHub.

The numbers are specific. For a calculation tied to inertial confinement fusion, the agents cut the combined cost metric by 11.8 times and reduced the required error-corrected qubits from 5,650 to 4,338. For simulating a light-sensitive molecule, they made the simulation eight times cheaper. For cytochrome P450, the enzyme that breaks down most medicines, they reported a 2.5 times improvement and cut qubits from 481 to 333. They also found a 2.57 times speedup for one implementation of Grover's search algorithm, and a 290 times speedup for arcsin, a routine that loads numbers into quantum states.

These are circuit-level resource estimates, not runs on working quantum machines, and the gains apply to the specific implementations the agents targeted. The more durable contribution may be the verification pipeline. If others can build on circuits that come with machine-checked proofs, AI-generated research gets a kind of checkability that most of it currently lacks.
takeaways: Anyone working on quantum resource estimation can clone the Lean library and check whether a proof covers the exact problem they care about.
stories.source_title: Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification
stories.author: Sergey Shirobokov et al.
stories.dek: The largest gain was a 290-fold speedup on one arithmetic routine, and the team is open-sourcing the verified library.

stories.headline: OpenAI and Cisco release Shirudo, an open-source eBPF runtime that shields Linux while patches roll out
body: OpenAI and Cisco have released Shirudo, an open-source runtime that lets operators place temporary protections on running Linux systems while a real patch is tested and rolled out. It uses eBPF, a Linux mechanism for small programs that run inside the kernel at chosen points, to observe suspicious activity and block specific code paths without restarting anything. In a controlled test, a shield generated with Codex stopped an exploit attempt against a live Elasticsearch service.

The problem it targets is the gap between disclosure and patching. Testing and deploying a patch can take days or weeks, and blocking a vulnerable operation outright can take a service down, because legitimate requests often use the same call. Shirudo lets teams watch how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it. Shields are cryptographically signed and checked by the eBPF verifier before loading, and a Trusted Platform Module records when protections are loaded or removed.

The authors want agents to take part. They describe programmable controls that would let an agent investigate a vulnerability, draft a targeted shield and check it against the exploit, with security teams approving what gets deployed. That approval step is the central safeguard in the design, and whether it holds up at machine speed in practice is the open question the project is now asking outside developers to help answer.
takeaways: If you run Linux services you cannot patch immediately, test whether a shield in monitor mode disrupts legitimate traffic before enforcing it.
stories.dek: In a controlled test, an AI-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit against a running Elasticsearch service without a restart.

stories.headline: XNU Linux loads Apple's XNU kernel code so macOS userspace programs can run on Linux
body: XNU Linux is a new open-source project that loads components of Apple's XNU kernel, the kernel behind macOS, into Linux as a loadable kernel module. According to the report's summary, the rest of the system stays unmodified on an ARM64 Linux machine. This story was written from the standfirst only, because the full article was not retrievable, so the compatibility claims have not been checked.

Running macOS userspace depends on far more than the kernel, including frameworks, libraries and system services, so the standfirst does not show how complete the compatibility is. Treat it as an experiment for now and check the specific macOS binaries you need before relying on it.
stories.source_title: XNU Linux Lets macOS Userspace Processes Run On Linux
stories.author: Michael Larabel
stories.dek: The project builds a Linux kernel module from Apple's open-source XNU components and aims to run macOS software on unmodified ARM64 Linux systems.

stories.headline: JDK 28 moves ZGC's heap preparation onto worker threads, so startup gets faster
body: JEP 545 is now integrated into JDK 28. It shifts heap acquisition and preparation away from the critical path of startup, handing it to concurrent worker threads, one per heap partition. Until now, ZGC users had to choose between a small initial heap, which started fast but warmed up slowly, and a large one with pre-touched memory, which warmed quickly but paid the full setup cost before the first request.

The new worker commits and uncommits memory as capacity changes, and pre-touches memory before application threads reach it, collapsing small pages into large ones along the way. On Linux 6.1 and later, ZGC can probe for the kernel's collapse mode and upgrade pages to 2 MB while the application runs, without an administrator reserving large pages in advance. The preparation budget is fixed at a quarter of available CPU, so it cannot take over the machine.

The headline startup numbers depend on a companion change, JEP 546, which adds adaptive heap sizing and still defaults to off. Teams that want the small initial heap the JEP measures need to enable that companion, and should benchmark their own warmup curves rather than assume the published figures carry over.
takeaways: Benchmark startup and warmup on JDK 28 with and without AlwaysPreTouch before changing heap flags in production.
stories.source_title: JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28
stories.author: A N M Bazlur Rahman
stories.dek: Startup with a 2 MB heap is measured in a fraction of a second, while a 32 GB heap takes more than ten seconds on current hardware.

stories.headline: Kubernetes 1.38 removes kubectl's WebSocket opt-outs and the kuberc name field
body: The Kubernetes release team has previewed v1.38, and it includes removals that will affect anything still relying on older settings. The kubectl environment variables that let users opt out of WebSockets for exec, attach, cp and port-forward will be removed. After that, kubectl will try WebSockets first and fall back to SPDY when needed. Scripts that set the variables will simply stop having any effect.

In kuberc, the name field on credential plugin allowlist entries was deprecated in v1.36 and will not appear in the stable kubectl.config.k8s.io/v1 API that arrives with v1.38. Entries that use name need to switch to command now. The preview warns that details may still change before release.

The longer-term change is cgroup v1. Since v1.35, kubelet refuses to start on cgroup v1 nodes unless failCgroupV1 is set to false. That setting still works in v1.38, but the team calls it a short-term fix, with removal of cgroup v1 support planned for a future release. Separately, an admission webhook change that has been on by default since v1.37 stops webhooks from receiving authentication and authorization review requests.
takeaways: Search your CI and scripts for the two WebSocket variables and for name fields in kuberc allowlist entries.
Check that your nodes already run cgroup v2, since the failCgroupV1 workaround is temporary.
stories.author: Aaron Braundmeier et al.
stories.dek: Two removals will break scripts that set old variables or use the name field, and the cgroup v1 deadline is closing.

stories.headline: NVIDIA's Nemotron-Labs-Sigma generates text by denoising embeddings instead of one token at a time
body: NVIDIA has released Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, 14 open checkpoints at 3B and 8B that generate text through continuous diffusion rather than predicting one token at a time. The model writes text in blocks, denoising compact token embeddings conditioned on the preceding context before reading out tokens. It is initialized from a pretrained autoregressive model, and the researchers report it is competitive with leading masked diffusion and autoregressive baselines, with its strongest gains on coding.

The efficiency claims are the part to check. Distillation for few-step generation produces eight tokens per pass on math and four on coding, and the authors say accuracy barely moves. The diffusion and autoregressive streams share a backbone, so the distilled model can draft blocks that the autoregressive side verifies, reproducing greedy output. The authors report that speedup on an NVIDIA GB200 with the 8B model.

What remains open is how these numbers hold outside NVIDIA's hardware and benchmark suites, and how well the embedding-space steering that the authors offer for trading quality against diversity works in practice. The open checkpoints let outside teams test both claims directly.
takeaways: Run the 8B checkpoint against your own coding tasks and compare output identity under the speculative setup before trusting the throughput figure.
stories.event: nvidia nemotron sigma diffusion language model
stories.source_title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron-Labs-Sigma Continuous Diffusion Language Models
stories.dek: The 8B model reached 3.46 times the throughput of plain autoregressive decoding on a GB200, with its diffusion stream drafting blocks for the autoregressive one to verify.

stories.headline: Tencent's Hy4 is an open-weight MoE model that reads images and video with a million-token context
body: The Tencent Hy Team has released Hy4, a mixture-of-experts flagship that handles text, images and video. The language backbone has 770 billion total parameters and activates 49 billion per token. Each MoE layer has 256 routed experts and one shared expert, and each token uses the top eight routed experts. A vision encoder with an adapter turns image and video frames into tokens the language model can process alongside text.

The architecture borrows from other recent open models. Attention uses a gated version of DeepSeek's sparse attention, with index reuse across layers, and the residual path uses hyper-connections to widen information flow between layers. Hy4 also includes a five-layer, 3.3-billion-parameter drafter that reuses the main model's KV cache for speculative decoding, which the team says keeps long-context drafting at a low, constant cost.

Tencent says Hy4 scales up both pretraining and post-training compared with its preview, and adds vision and computer-use abilities for command-line and graphical tasks. The base-model results carry a caveat from the authors: the base model was trained on a lot of synthetic instruction data, so it sometimes ignores the expected answer format in few-shot tests, which can distort the scores. Independent evaluations will say more than the company's own tables.
takeaways: Check Hy4's reported few-shot scores against an instruction-tuned evaluation before comparing it with other open models.
stories.source_title: Tencent Releases Hy4 With Multimodal Input and Million-Token Context
stories.dek: The 770-billion-parameter model activates 49 billion parameters per token and ships with a built-in drafter for speculative decoding.
